newsitem.title: south korea: INTERVIEW-Daewoo eyes global expansion.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Daewoo eyes global expansion.

text.p: South Korea's Daewoo Group will soon be assembling cars in China, selling cars in the United States and sending hundreds of its top executives to beachheads worldwide, the group's brash chairman said on Monday.
"Global expansion has emerged as an issue of survival for us," Kim Woo-choong said in an interview with Reuters.
Expanding overseas has become a life-and-death issue for South Korean companies, which are suffering increasingly from tightening demand at home, he said.
The indefatigable head of South Korea's fourth-largest group said he was confident of being able to build a car assembly plant with an annual capacity of 200,000 units in China by 1999.
"Why should we be building a large-scale car part plant in China unless we want to produce finished cars there," Kim said.
Daewoo is scheduled to complete a parts plant in Shandong Province by 1999, which can produce 300,000 engines and transmissions annually.
"I've been in China more than 100 times to push the car project," Kim said, at times gesticulating enthusiastically.
He said he could see China's per-capita income rising to $10,000 by 2010, which would expand its car market to 15 million cars a year, similar to that of the U.S. or western Europe now.
Kim said the plant, if realised, would be built in a joint venture with one of China's three carmakers.

Setting his sights on the giant U.S. market, he said Daewoo would set up 50 direct U.S. sales outlets and begin selling cars in the U.S. either in October or February, depending on how the group sets its sales strategy.
"The U.S. is the most difficult market. We don't expect to make money by selling cars there in the short term. But we will prove we can make good cars," Kim said.
It is a tall order, as South Korean cars are viewed as low-priced and low quality among demanding U.S. consumers.
On the controversial issue of excess capacity, Kim said that was a problem for advanced countries, whose markets had reached saturation, but not for South Korea.
"I don't think manufacturers in advanced nations can complain about our expansion because it is focused largely on emerging markets, which are growing rapidly," Kim said.
World-wide vehicle demand would double to 100 million units a year in 10 years with most new purchases coming from developing nations like China and India, he said.

As a step towards Kim's goal of globalisation, he said he would set up 20 independent groups around the world to strengthen the group's overseas operations. The overseas groups will generally operate independently of Seoul headquarters, he said.
"I think it would better to have permanent localised business headquarters around the world, because we want to grow together with the host nations," Kim said.
He said Daewoo would have about 1,000 overseas business sites by 2000, including production bases, sales outlets and wholly-owned companies, up from about 500 now.
"About half of Daewoo's 1,200 executives will be posted overseas to utilise their expertise," he said.
Kim said the group's total sales would rise about 25 percent this year from $68 billion in 1996. The group's sales expanded 33 percent in 1996 from the previous year.
Daewoo's car sales in eastern Europe and the Commonwealth of Independent States would reach 500,000 units this year from almost nothing last year, he said.
"Daewoo will rank as the largest car seller in the region," he said.
